newsitem.title: UK: Rights groups urge more Bosnia war crime arrests.
newsitem.headline: Rights groups urge more Bosnia war crime arrests.

text.p: Human rights groups joined forces on Friday to launch a worldwide "Arrest now" campaign to speed up the capture of indicted war criminals in former Yugoslavia.

Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Institute for War and Peace called on NATO countries to order their peacekeeping forces to arrest the 66 officially-listed war criminals still at large.

"While (the war criminals) remain free to carry out political activities, national reconciliation is being seriously jeopardised and the entire peace process in Bosnia-Herzegovina risks unravelling again into a repetition of the atrocities that shocked the world," said a joint statement read out at a news conference.

Timed to coincide with the second anniversary of the July 11 fall of Srebrenica, the launch of "Arrest Now" follows the shooting of one suspected war criminal and the arrest of another by British troops in the northern Bosnian town of Prijedor.

Amnesty said thousands of civilians were believed to have been slaughtered after the capture of the so-called 'safe area' of Srebrenica by Bosnian Serbs in July 1995, and it noted that the vast majority of those responsible for the killings were still at large.
"Their liberty puts the whole international community to shame," the statement said.

Of 75 war criminals named by the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague, only nine have been arrested. Most remain in Bosnia-Herzegovina, with 51 believed to be living in entity of Republica Srpska, which refuses to cooperate with the tribunal.

On Thursday, Bosnian Serb Simo Drljaca, who is alleged to have led brutal ethnic cleansing operations against Moslems and Croat civilians, was shot dead after he fired at the NATO troops trying to arrest him.
Hospital director Milan Kovacevic was arrested and will be tried by the United Nations war tribunal in The Hague.
Although neither was named in the official list of war crimes published by the tribunal, they had been listed in sealed indictments, officials said.
"What happened yesterday was hugely important, but it is just the beginning," said Amnesty's Director of Legal and International Organisations Program, Nicholas Howen.
"What we need to see now is not just part-time justice but full time justice."

Howen said with only 11 months left before the multinational Stabilisation Force (SFOR) peacekeeping mandate was due to expire, NATO soldiers would have to arrest more than one war criminal every week in order to get through the official list.
A former BBC correspondent in wartime Sarajevo and recently-elected parliamentarian, Martin Bell, praised Thursday's action.
"What happened yesterday was a positive symbol," he told the news conference. "We would like to see that all nations are equally on board and committed to this process."
An open letter signed by prominent individuals and National Government Organisations was released at the London gathering urging political leaders to apprehend the war criminals.
